events.text:
# A Name from the County Line: The Greyerbiehl Years at the 2 A.M. Club

## Before the Greyerbiehls

The sources do not give a date for when the bar on the corner of Miller and Montford became the 2 A.M. Club, but they do sketch what came before. In 1988 Mary Greyerbiehl told the Record that

events.quote: Before it was the 2 A M. Club, the bar was owned by Bill Brown and called “The Little Brown Jug."

events.text: before it was the 2 A M. Club, the bar was owned by Bill Brown and called "The Little Brown Jug."

events.quote: It was first a grocery store but, during Prohibition, sold little bottles of booze called Mickeys hidden behind cans of food on the shelves.

events.text: It was first a grocery store but, during Prohibition, sold little bottles of booze called Mickeys hidden behind cans of food on the shelves.
The Record's 1979 farewell to Bill Greyerbiehl, surviving only in fragments, says

events.quote: The bar had been a grocery store before 1932. but opened in ’33 by Bill … before 1932. but opened in ’33 by Bill Brown and Joe Hornsby.

events.text: the bar had been a grocery store before 1932. but opened in '33 by Bill Brown and Joe Hornsby.
The same 1979 fragments hint at the name's origin. The bar stood

events.quote: The bar had been a grocery … on county ground and Mill Valley had an ordinance that required all bars to shut down at midnight.

events.text: on county ground and Mill Valley had an ordinance that required all bars to shut down at midnight.
A broken line follows:

events.quote: "We were the only one open … the Tamalpais High class of '3l.

events.text: "We were the only one open

. The sources suggest the name came from the club's place outside town limits, where it could stay open later than Mill Valley's bars. The published history makes the same link when it says that after annexation

events.quote: Either way, the 2 A.M. Club had become a Mill Valley bar, with nothing left of the boundary but its name.

events.text: the 2 A.M. Club had become a Mill Valley bar, with nothing left of the boundary but its name.
By early 1940 the name was in use. That year Bill Greyerbiehl recalled:

events.quote: When Nick Standish and Pete Star said they were selling, we were ready."

events.text: "When Nick Standish and Pete Star said they were selling, we were ready."

## A family buys in

Bill Greyerbiehl

events.quote: Bill Greyerbiehl grew up in Larkspur, graduated from Tamalpais High in 1931, worked at the Langendorf bakery in the Depression and tended bar in Larkspur before moving to Mill Valley in 1937.

events.text: grew up in Larkspur, graduated from Tamalpais High in 1931, worked at the Langendorf bakery in the Depression and tended bar in Larkspur before moving to Mill Valley in 1937.
He came first as a regular:

events.quote: “I was a customer every night,” he said.

events.text: "I was a customer every night," he said.

events.quote: When Pete Starr gave up the club early in 1940, Bill, his younger brother Breslin, called Bres, and their father Louis bought it together.

events.text: When Pete Starr gave up the club early in 1940, Bill, his younger brother Breslin, called Bres, and their father Louis bought it together.
Their father,

events.quote: Louis Greyerbiehl had been born in Canada in 1885, and with his sons he had run the Twin Cities Mattress Company.

events.text: Louis Greyerbiehl had been born in Canada in 1885, and with his sons he had run the Twin Cities Mattress Company.

events.quote: By early 1941 the family was advertising in the Record: “For good refreshments anytime, join the gang at 2 A. M. Club, Miller & Montford, Greyerbiehl & Sons”.

events.text: By early 1941 the family was advertising in the Record: "For good refreshments anytime, join the gang at 2 A. M. Club, Miller & Montford, Greyerbiehl & Sons".
The place

events.quote: The place they bought was a workingman’s tavern and stayed one.

events.text: was a workingman's tavern and stayed one
. Bill remembered

events.quote: Bill remembered beer for a dime and whiskey at fifteen cents a shot; a kitchen serving sandwiches and chili beans, because “you had to serve food”; and doors that opened at six in the morning, “a lot of people drank during the day then.

events.text: beer for a dime and whiskey at fifteen cents a shot
, along with

events.quote: There was a hardwood floor for dancing, a piano, and a back room for poker, with the fireplace “as hot as the card games”.

events.text: a hardwood floor for dancing, a piano, and a back room for poker
. The family did not own the land underneath:

events.quote: The Lenherr brothers, who ran the service station, owned the club’s corner too.Miller Avenue at La Goma Street, 1940s.

events.text: the Lenherr brothers, who ran the service station, owned the club's corner too.

## The war years

The war took both sons away. Louis

events.quote: He was running it when burglars emptied three amusement machines in February 1943.

events.text: was running it when burglars emptied three amusement machines in February 1943.
He died that August, and his funeral notice described him as

events.quote: Death Summons L. Greyerbiehl On Saturday • FUNERAL SERVICES for Louis Greyerbiehl, 58, operator of the “Two A, M.” club on Miller avenue at Locust, who died suddenly of a heart attack at his home at 20 Montford avenue, Saturday, will be cosducted Friday morning at 9 o’clock from Keaton’s mortuary, S

events.text: operator of the "Two A, M." club on Miller avenue at Locust
. It also recorded that his sons were

events.quote: and by two sons, Wilbur and Breslin, who are both in the service.

events.text: both in the service.
That leaves a gap: who kept the bar open while both sons were away? Search snippets from the Record point to a third family member. An October 1943 notice lists

events.quote: A M Club"] ... follows: Frances, Wilbur L. & Bros E, Greyerbiehl DBA Two A. M, Club Miller Ave. & Richardson Street Mill ... [query Greyerbiehl] ... described … text not downloaded) https://cdnc.ucr.edu/?a=d&d=MVR19431014.2.75.2 [query"Two A M Club"] ... follows: Frances, Wilbur L. & Bros E, Greyerb

events.text: Frances, Wilbur L. & Bros E, Greyerbiehl DBA Two A. M, Club
. Frances was Louis's widow, named in the funeral notice as

events.quote: SURVIVORS Mr. Greyerbiehl is survived by his wife, Mrs. Prances Greyerbiehl.

events.text: his wife, Mrs. Prances Greyerbiehl.
A January 1945 advertisement for

events.quote: The 2 A. M. CLUB A Friendly WORKINGMAN'S TAVERN OPEN 10 ... [query Greyerbiehl] ... WORKINGMAN'S TAVERN OPEN 10 A.M. to 12 MIDNIGHT Frances Greyerbiehl Bill Greyerbiehl In … Page 5 Advertisements Column 2 [ADVERTISEMENT] (CDNC search snippets only; full text not downloaded) https://cdnc.ucr.edu/?a=d

events.text: A Friendly WORKINGMAN'S TAVERN OPEN 10 A.M. to 12 MIDNIGHT

names both Frances and Bill. The published histories do not discuss her role. Probably she held the business on paper during the war, but the sources do not say who stood behind the bar.

Bill

events.quote: GREYERBIEHL RETURNS TO MILL VALLEY Bill Greyerbiehl has returned to Mill Valley after nearly two years of service in the radio section of the air service command and has resumed the management of the 2 A. M. club at Locust.

events.text: returned to Mill Valley after nearly two years of service in the radio section of the air service command and has resumed the management of the 2 A. M. club
in December 1944. Bres

events.quote: Bres Greyerbiehl Back From Army • BRES Greyerbiehl, just out of the army after four years of service, much of which was overseas, has returned to Mill Valley and joined his brother, Bill Greyerbiehl, in operation of the 2 A. M. Club at Locust.

events.text: just out of the army after four years of service, much of which was overseas, has returned to Mill Valley and joined his brother

in March 1946.

## Two brothers on Miller Avenue

The brothers ran the club together for three decades. In 1945, after a remodel, the club reopened with walls that

events.quote: The walls were blue, the light was indirect, and the bar was Philippine mahogany.

events.text: were blue, the light was indirect, and the bar was Philippine mahogany.
In May 1948

events.quote: Bill and Bress Greyerbiehl of the 2 A. M. club are holding a “television preview" tonight.

events.text: Bill and Bress Greyerbiehl of the 2 A. M. club are holding a "television preview"
for a set installed

events.quote: While there are no actual television broadcasts in this area, authorities envision telecasts locally in the near future.

events.text: while there are no actual television broadcasts in this area

.

The family team included Bill's wife Mary.

events.quote: Mary Galeotti, a Mill Valley native, came into the bar in 1940; they married in May 1946.

events.text: Mary Galeotti, a Mill Valley native, came into the bar in 1940; they married in May 1946.

events.quote: She tended bar at the 2 A.M. on Sunday afternoons while Bill and Bres, the regular bartenders, played baseball on the empty lot that later became the Safeway.

events.text: She tended bar at the 2 A.M. on Sunday afternoons while Bill and Bres, the regular bartenders, played baseball on the empty lot that later became the Safeway.
Regulars knew the place as

events.quote: Club at the corner of Miller and Montford avenues, across and down the street from her and her husband Bill’s house on Montford Bill, his brother, Bres, and their father, Louis Greyerbiehl, owned the bar — known to its regulars as “The Deuce" — for 40 years.

events.text: "The Deuce"
. Its sign served as a landmark, and directions to Muir Woods said to

events.quote: People asking the way to Muir Woods were told to go down Miller and “turn at the 2 A. M. club”.

events.text: "turn at the 2 A. M. club"

events.quote: Bres Greyerbiehl was co-owner of the 2 A.M. Club with his brother for 36 years.

events.text: Bres Greyerbiehl was co-owner of the 2 A.M. Club with his brother for 36 years.

events.quote: He died in June 1976, at 58, leaving his wife Nancy.

events.text: He died in June 1976, at 58
. Bill carried on alone for three more years. In June 1979 he announced the sale:

events.quote: “My friends don’t like it, but a guy’s got to retire,” the 65-year old Mill Valleyan said.

events.text: "My friends don't like it, but a guy's got to retire,"
said the 65-year-old. The buyers were

events.quote: They are Tom Gootherts, a bartender at the Brother’s Bar and Richard Mattos, owner of the Miller Ave. 711 store.

events.text: Tom Gootherts, a bartender at the Brother's Bar and Richard Mattos, owner of the Miller Ave. 711 store.
Bill

events.quote: He died in September 1990, at 76.

events.text: died in September 1990, at 76.

## What the sources don't say

- **When the club was renamed.** No passage dates the change from Bill Brown's "Little Brown Jug" to the 2 A.M. Club. The sources also never state the name's origin outright; the closing-hour explanation is an inference from fragmentary text.
- **Opening date and purchase year.** The 1979 article puts the bar's opening in 1933. The family's purchase is dated 1940 in most sources but 1939 in the 1988 interview. The 1988 interview also says the family owned the bar for 40 years, while other sources say 39.
- **Who bought it.** Bill's 1990 obituary says

events.quote: He and his brother, Breslin Greyerbiehl, bought the 2 A.M. Club in 1940.

events.text: He and his brother, Breslin Greyerbiehl, bought the 2 A.M. Club in 1940.

It leaves out Louis, whom the other accounts include.
- **Frances Greyerbiehl's role.** Her part in running the bar in 1943–45 appears only in search snippets of legal notices and ads and deserves a closer look.
- **Annexation year.** Bill remembered it as 1949 or 1950, the bar's website gives 1951, and the council moved on it in November 1950.

gaps.title: The closing-hour law and the annexation
gaps.description: The bar’s name rests on Mill Valley’s early closing hour, but the date and terms of the ordinance (10 p.m. or midnight) and the year the Miller Avenue strip was annexed to the city are not settled.
gaps.fill: Ask the Lucretia Little History Room about city ordinances and council minutes of the late 1930s and the annexation years (not verified: check with them); read the Mill Valley Record for those years on CDNC.
gaps.why: Could pin down the closing-hour ordinance behind the club's name and settle the conflicting annexation dates (1949, 1950 or 1951).

gaps.title: The Independent Journal for 1949 to 2001 has not been read
gaps.description: The Mill Valley papers on CDNC carry the bar’s story to the early 2000s, but the county daily’s police, court and license news for these decades has not been searched.
gaps.fill: Search the Independent-Journal of 1949 to 1978 in NewspaperArchive with an SFPL card, or in the free Internet Archive scans of those years; read 1979 to 2001 on microfilm at the Anne T. Kent California Room.
gaps.why: The county daily's license notices might date the change from the Little Brown Jug to the 2 A.M. Club and confirm the ownership transfers.

gaps.title: No interviews with owners, staff or regulars
gaps.description: Nobody who ran, worked at or drank at the bar has been interviewed for this history.
gaps.fill: Ask the Lucretia Little History Room whether its oral-history collection includes the Greyerbiehls or other Homestead families (not verified: check with them).
gaps.why: Interviews could clarify how Frances, Bill, Bres and Mary actually divided the work during and after the war.

gaps.title: Owners, sales and the building
gaps.description: The sales of 1934, 1979, 2010 and about 2021 are known from the papers and later accounts, but the deeds, the earlier owners of the lot and the building’s date are not.
gaps.fill: Search the Marin County Recorder’s grantor and grantee indexes for 380 Miller Avenue (its details need checking with the office), and ask the Anne T. Kent California Room about property research (it takes questions by parcel number).

gaps.title: The San Francisco papers have not been searched
gaps.description: Herb Caen and other Chronicle writers mentioned the bar, and the Examiner covered the 1906 to 1910 Homestead license fights, but neither paper was searched for this history.
gaps.fill: Search the Chronicle (NewsBank) and the Examiner (ProQuest) with an SFPL card; see the library-card databases guide.

gaps.title: The Huey Lewis and the News “Sports” cover shoot
gaps.description: Who took the 1983 cover photograph at the bar, on what day, and which regulars appear in it are not in the sources read.
gaps.fill: Search the Chronicle for 1983 and 1984 in NewsBank, and ask the Lucretia Little History Room whether it holds anything on the shoot (not verified: check with them).

gaps.title: Two Mill Valley Historical Society pieces have not been read
gaps.description: The Mill Valley Historical Society’s “Vignette” on the 2AM Club (2014) and its “Homestead in the Thirties” (2012) were found by title but not read.
gaps.fill: Ask the Lucretia Little History Room whether it holds the Society’s publications (not verified: check with them), or ask the Mill Valley Historical Society.

gaps.title: Why the state moved against the license in 2009 and 2010
gaps.description: A 2018 interview says state agents threatened the liquor license after reports of drug use, which forced the 2010 sale. The violations, dates and penalty are not in any source read.
gaps.fill: Search the Marin Independent Journal for 2009 and 2010 in NewsBank (SFPL card). License history is kept by the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control (not verified: check with them).

anne-t-kent.name: Anne T. Kent California Room, Marin County Free Library
anne-t-kent.address: Civic Center Library, 3501 Civic Center Drive, Room 427, San Rafael, CA 94903
anne-t-kent.hours: Monday–Friday 9:00 AM–6:00 PM; closed Saturday and Sunday. Survey Map & Special Collections Annex open to the public Thursdays 1–5 pm. Holiday closures are listed on the location page.
anne-t-kent.appointment: Appointments are not necessary but helpful, because some materials are off site and need 24–48 hours' notice to retrieve. To visit the Map Annex by appointment, email the California Room.
anne-t-kent.request_method: Email californiaroom@marincounty.gov or use the online form (property, genealogy, local history, obituary and other questions) to send research requests and ask for off-site items to be pulled. Give 24–48 hours' notice for off-site materials. Include names, addresses, dates and APNs in your question.
tips: Email ahead: off-site materials need 24–48 hours' notice.
Unrecorded maps and surveys are in the Survey Map & Special Collections Annex, open Thursdays 1–5 pm.
The Digital Archive (photos, postcards, interviews, ephemera) is linked from the California Room page.

library-card-databases.request_method: Free to all California residents. Apply online (or on a paper application at a branch), then visit any SFPL location in person with valid ID to receive the card. SFPL does not issue eCards online. Database links go through SFPL's sign-in page (ezproxy.sfpl.org): enter your complete 14-digit library card number (barcode) and PIN.

marin-county-recorder.request_method: Contact the library to arrange access.

marin-history-museum.name: Marin History Museum Research Library
marin-history-museum.address: Boyd Gate House, 1125 B Street, San Rafael, CA
marin-history-museum.hours: Wednesday & Friday, 11 am–3 pm (and by appointment).
marin-history-museum.appointment: No appointment is stated for library hours; appointments can be made in advance for visits outside library hours.
marin-history-museum.request_method: Submit a Research Request online or email research@marinhistory.org. Ready-reference questions are free but limited; longer requests may be charged $25 per half hour, and you will be contacted first if your request goes beyond ready reference. Materials may only be used inside the library during library hours.
marin-history-museum.reproductions: High-resolution digital scans of photographs are available for purchase: submit a Photo Request Form to info@marinhistory.org (or by mail), or call 415-382-1182 for an in-person appointment. See the museum's list of fees.
tips: The whole collection is searchable in the museum's Online Catalog before you go.
The library is open only Wednesday and Friday, 11 am–3 pm, so email research@marinhistory.org ahead.

mill-valley-history-room.name: Lucretia Little History Room, Mill Valley Public Library
mill-valley-history-room.address: Mill Valley Public Library, 375 Throckmorton Avenue, Mill Valley, CA 94941
mill-valley-history-room.hours: Monday by appointment; Tuesday & Wednesday 10am–4pm; Thursday, Friday & Saturday 1pm–4pm; Sunday closed. Hours are subject to change (closes at 2pm on Wednesday, November 25).
mill-valley-history-room.appointment: Research visits beyond general browsing must be scheduled in advance; call or email to make sure staff are available. To see archival materials or get staff help, complete a Research Request Form before your visit.
mill-valley-history-room.request_method: Fill out the History Room Research Request Form before your visit if you want archival materials pulled or staff assistance, then confirm a time by phone or email. The collection is non-circulating and used on site only. Many items are digitized and searchable in the Digital Collections catalog.
mill-valley-history-room.reproductions: Researchers are welcome to make photocopies and take photographs of items in the collection, pending exceptions. Digitized public-domain materials online may be used freely without permission; please credit the History Room.
mill-valley-history-room.permissions: No permission is needed for fair use or public-domain material. If the History Room holds copyright and your use exceeds fair use, its permission is required; for third-party copyright, ask the rights holder. Preferred credit: "Courtesy of the Lucretia Little History Room, Mill Valley Public Library."
tips: Search the Digital Collections at mvpl.catalogaccess.com before visiting.
Send the Research Request Form ahead; Monday visits are by appointment only.

sfpl.name: San Francisco History Center, San Francisco Public Library
sfpl.address: San Francisco History Center, 6th Floor, Main Library, 100 Larkin Street, San Francisco, CA 94102
sfpl.request_method: Most materials are non-circulating and used in the History Center on the 6th floor. Many books, periodicals and some archival collections are in the SFPL online catalog; other materials are not fully catalogued, so ask a librarian (415-557-4567 or sfhistory@sfpl.org) before you go. For high-resolution photo scans, email the Reproduction of Images form to sfphoto@sfpl.org.
sfpl.reproductions: Low-resolution images on digitalsf.org may be downloaded free for personal or classroom use. High-resolution TIFFs: submit one Reproduction of Images form listing Photo ID numbers to sfphoto@sfpl.org; existing digital files $15 (300 dpi), new scans $20–$50; prepayment required; existing files take 1–2 weeks, new scans 3–4 weeks.
sfpl.permissions: Images are for personal use only; any publication, exhibit or other use requires prior written permission from the San Francisco History Center via its permissions forms.
sfpl.bring: For a library card: a valid photo ID, presented in person (cards are free to all California residents).
tips: A free SFPL card is open to all California residents: apply online, then show photo ID at any branch.
SFPL's Access World News (NewsBank) includes digital replicas of current papers including the Marin Independent Journal and San Francisco Chronicle.
Many holdings are not in the catalog; ask a librarian about card indexes and folder lists.
